                    ### Question
                    A 6-month-old infant male is brought to the emergency department with a 1-hour history of vomiting and convulsions. He was born at home and had sporadic prenatal care though his parents say that he appeared healthy at birth. He initially fed well; however, his parents have noticed that he has been feeding poorly and is very irritable since they moved on to baby foods. They have also noticed mild yellowing of his skin but assumed it would go away over time. On presentation, he is found to be very sleepy, and physical exam reveals an enlarged liver and spleen. The rest of the physical exam is normal. Which of the following enzymes is most likely functioning abnormally in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Aldolase B
opb. Fructokinase
opc. Gal-1-phosphate uridyl transferase
opd. Galactokinase deficiency
ope. Lactase

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of the 6-month-old infant, including vomiting, irritability, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly, strongly suggests a metabolic disorder, specifically galactosemia. The symptoms of poor feeding and irritability, along with the observed jaundice, indicate possible galactose accumulation due to impaired metabolism. The enzyme most commonly associated with classic galactosemia is Gal-1-phosphate uridyl transferase, which is responsible for converting galactose-1-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate. The presence of hepatosplenomegaly and jaundice aligns with liver dysfunction due to galactose accumulation. Therefore, the most likely enzyme functioning abnormally in this patient is Gal-1-phosphate uridyl transferase. Evidence paths indicating the relationship between metabolic diseases and symptoms like vomiting and hepatosplenomegaly further support this conclusion.
